passages: The successful impact of the DART spacecraft with Dimorphos and the resulting change in the orbit of Dimorphos7 demonstrates that kinetic impactor technology is a viable technique to potentially defend Earth if necessary.

Here we report the DART spacecraft’s autonomous kinetic impact into Dimorphos and reconstruct the impact event, including the timeline leading to impact, the location and nature of the DART impact site, and the size and shape of Dimorphos.

The blocky nature of the impact site probably influenced crater formation, ejecta and momentum enhancement, as seen in impact experiments28,32,33,34, numerical simulations25,35 and the Small Carry-on Impactor experiment on Hayabusa25.DART did not measure the mass of Dimorphos.
NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission is a full-scale test of kinetic impact technology.

passages: Asteroids, comets and Kuiper belt Astrophysical dust Rings and moons Asteroid Dynamics and Impact Processes MainNASA’s DART successfully impacted Dimorphos, the secondary of the near-Earth binary asteroid (65803) Didymos, on 26 September 2022 at 23:14 UTC.
Orbital period change of Dimorphos due to the DART kinetic impact.
Here we report the change in the orbital period of Dimorphos as a result of the DART kinetic impact to be −33.0 ± 1.0 (3σ) min.
The primary objective of DART was to change the orbital period of Dimorphos around Didymos to demonstrate that a kinetic impactor is a viable method of asteroid deflection1,7.

Data availability The lightcurves and radar data used in this analysis of the orbital period are available in the JHU/APL Data Archive at https://lib.jhuapl.edu/papers/orbital-period-change-of-dimorphos-due-to-the-dart/.

If the incident momentum from the impacting spacecraft was simply transferred to the asteroid target with no further momentum enhancement, an orbital period change for Dimorphos of roughly 7 min was expected1.

passages: On 26 September 2022 the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft impacted Dimorphos, a satellite of the asteroid 65803 Didymos.
Here we report optical observations of Dimorphos before, during and after the impact, from a network of citizen science telescopes across the world.
We estimate lower limits on the mass contained in the ejecta, which was 0.3 - 0.5% Dimorphos' mass depending on the dust size.
We also observe a reddening of the ejecta upon impact.
In nominal cases, pre-impact predictions of the orbital period reduction ranged from ~8.8 - 17.2 minutes.
We find a maximum brightening of 2.29 $\pm$ 0.14 mag upon impact.
